sangx: A Home-Grown Web Server (nginx Rewrite) Plan

StatusThe plan is complete but the project has not been proposed or started (on 2026-10-28 the user proposed "build our own nginx" and three discussions — feasibility, configuration, and security — were completed; this page is the authoritative record of their conclusions). The project is named sangx (sa + ngx, decided by the user on 2026-10-28). Prerequisites: STD completion wave two wraps up + the reverse-proxy handler model is ruled on. The phases and the items awaiting ruling are updated on this page on a rolling basis.

Motivation: Why Not Use nginx Itself

  • Its configuration is structurally inhumane: as soon as add_header appears in a child block it wipes out all inheritance from the parent block, if is officially acknowledged as evil, location precedence among exact/prefix/regex matches must be memorized, variables are lazily evaluated and only have values in specific phases, and there are no functions/loops/real expressions. The industry generally generates nginx.conf with template engines, which amounts to admitting the format cannot be written directly.
  • Its extension model is behind: nginx modules are C code running in-process with full privileges; OpenResty's Lua is likewise full-privilege. The SA ecosystem already has a more modern form: plugins divided by kind, two layers of permission — confirmation at install time ∩ policy at runtime — and a VM capability model.
  • The foundation is already in place: this is the natural endpoint of the "all basic cores built into sa_std" policy — the HTTP core was taken back into std in its day precisely because it failed at the plugin boundary (2026-10-24), and writing the server itself with the same std is the obvious implication.

Feasibility Mapping (against sci main 9dedd406 and the STD wave-two work in progress)

Existing Surfaces (Most of nginx's Foundation)

  • Protocol cores: HTTP/1.1 server + client, HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC sessions, WebSocket (including over unix), TCP/UDP, DTLS — judged an area of overtaking by multiple census lines.
  • The TLS configuration surface (landed in STD wave one): SNI, ALPN, peer certificates, mTLS, start_tls, session resumption — the core surface of nginx's ssl module.
  • Events and concurrency: the SLA async/task model, netx io_uring, process spawn, timers.
  • Tool surfaces: compression, sa_regex, TOML reading and writing, the IP/CIDR value layer (ACL/geo matching primitives), DNS record-type queries (upstream resolver primitives).
  • In production in STD wave two: generic sockopt passthrough (including SO_REUSEPORT), the proxy surface, SSE parsing, bit-level packing.

Gaps (Classified by Nature)

  • The reverse-proxy handler/hook model (the only architecture-level gap): one of the three suspended architecture rulings. nginx itself is the template — its 11 phase handlers + filter chain are a hook model validated over twenty years, so the ruling can be drafted in its shape, benefiting CXU and this project alike.
  • State shared across workers: the counterpart of nginx shared zones (rate-limit counters, upstream health, SSL session caches). SA currently has in-process globals; either an inter-process shmem surface must be added, or a single-process event-loop + thread-pool model can sidestep it — to be ruled on after load testing.
  • The sendfile/zero-copy send path: the lifeline of static-file throughput; whether std already has it remains to be checked (the census did not name it separately), and if not, it can be added as a small direct item.
  • Protocol client tails: FastCGI/uWSGI/SCGI — pure protocol work, of the same kind as STD wave two's SMTP line, to be filled in mechanically.
  • HTTP caching: fs + locks + expiration management; large in volume but with no architecture risk, belonging to the module layer.

Configuration Design: A Declaration Layer + a Code Layer

  • Declaration layer (90% of scenarios): structured data (TOML); server/listen/root/upstream are just form-filling; there are no inheritance traps, and missing fields and type errors are reported at load time with source locations.
  • Code layer (logic scenarios): the configuration itself is an SLA program — functions, loops, conditions, and environment-dependent branches are all available, compiled + type-checked at startup (a respectable version of nginx -t). An ACL can directly write a real expression such as ip_in_cidr(req.ip, ip_prefix_parse("10.0.0.0/8")), reusing the ip.sla value layer, instead of stitching variables together in a geo block.
  • Evaluation order is explicit, with no lazy-variable quirks: the soil for nginx's many "only triggered by specific configuration combinations" defects disappears here (see the security section).

Extension Design: VM Plugins

  • Four hook categories: phase handlers, filters, upstream balancers, and variable/directive extensions, registered into the phase model.
  • Two distribution tiers: hot paths (filters, balancing algorithms) use natively compiled plugins; the logic layer (authentication, dynamic routing, canary releases) uses SAB bytecode plugins running on the SA VM — change the logic without recompiling the server, hot-load a new generation, and let old connections drain on the old generation (borrowing nginx reload's generational model).
  • The permission cage: reuses the plugin system's already-decided two layers of permission (the permissions.lock confirmation at install time ∩ the runtime policy) and the VM's fs/net capability model — a reverse-proxy plugin by default has only net outbound access, and touching the file system requires separate confirmation. A VM plugin trap kills only itself, not the worker (an isolation C modules cannot give).
  • Ecosystem reuse: the same sap plugin format and confirmation flow as CXU; plugins from the CXU side can be mounted directly (such as jev decision-style upstream selection, or audited route changes via the VM tool surface).

The Security Argument: A Classification Ruling on nginx's Vulnerability History

Based on the full set of nginx's official security_advisories (2009–2026). Its vulnerability history is highly concentrated by class; this project rules on each class as follows:

  • Memory corruption class (the absolute mainstay: the chunked stack overflow CVE-2013-2028, SPDY CVE-2014-0133, the mp4 module repeatedly six or more times, the resolver family including the one-byte overwrite CVE-2021-23017, and UAFs in SSI/AIO/HTTP3 still appearing today; with extremely long latency — the alias+rewrite overflow fixed in 2026-10 had been latent for 21 years, in affected versions since 0.1.29): constructively eliminated for the most part, with consequences lowered by two grades. The SLA layer has no raw pointer arithmetic (the PTR macros are an explicit exception), ownership + the referee seal off UAFs, and out-of-bounds access degenerates into a trap — bugs of this class drop from RCE to a worker crash (DoS grade). The TCB boundary must be drawn clearly: the dividend covers only the SLA layer; the underlying Zig runtime and the linked OpenSSL are not within the dividend, and their CVE streams are inherited as-is.
  • Integer/logic errors → information disclosure (representative: the range filter integer overflow CVE-2017-7529): a language cannot save you from "computing it wrong", but it cuts the chain from "computed wrong → read memory outside the cache", so on its own it amounts to at most a wrong response. The countermeasure is engineering discipline: range-style logic is checked against fixed vectors, and all parsers (HTTP/QUIC/DNS wire) are under fuzz testing from day one.
  • Protocol state machine DoS (the HTTP/2 resource exhaustion family CVE-2018-16843/44, 2019-9511/9513/9516, and the protocol-level Rapid Reset): unrelated to language — any implementation will run into it; this is the one class where we gain no advantage; the countermeasure is to write the whole family checklist (stream reset rates, header limits, connection-level quotas) into the design and the acceptance cases, rather than patching them one by one after the fact.
  • Configuration-combination-triggered class: nginx's lazy variable evaluation + the implicit ordering of its scripting engine are its soil; once configuration is code, the soil is much smaller. The flip side must be admitted: user configuration logic enters the TCB, so plugins must have a capability cage + trap isolation.
  • New risks specific to this project (not hidden): the compiler enters the TCB — a referee misjudgment (proven by the AW line on 2026-10-28: structs with multiple String fields read/moved through & were systematically misjudged) can make safe source produce unsafe output; and the VM interpreter's stability has registered problems (the SAB interpreter segfaults on & scalar arguments). The overall ledger: vulnerability classes migrate as a whole — from memory corruption that can reach RCE, to logic errors that reach at most DoS + toolchain risk; the harm drops systematically by one grade, at the cost of the audit surface expanding to the compiler.

Phases (Suggested)

  • M0: static file service + two-layer configuration + access logs (this phase verifies the sendfile gap).
  • M1: reverse proxy + upstream load balancing and health checks (consumes the handler ruling).
  • M2: TLS/HTTP2 across the board + limit_req/limit_conn (consumes the shared-state ruling).
  • M3: HTTP caching + the FastCGI/uWSGI protocol tails.
  • Acceptance criteria for each phase: behavior comparison (with nginx itself as the reference), protocol flooding cases, parser fuzz rounds, and same-machine load-test comparisons against nginx (in the two scenarios of static files and reverse proxying).

List of Items Awaiting Ruling

  • Project name: sangx (decided, 2026-10-28).
  • The reverse-proxy handler/hook model (drafted on nginx's phase model; the ruling is shared with CXU).
  • The shared-state model: add a std shmem surface vs. sidestep with a single-process model.
  • The process model: multi-process SO_REUSEPORT (nginx-style) vs. single-process event loop + thread pool, to be decided after M0/M1 load testing.
  • Project start timing: after STD wave two wraps up.
